Gastroenterology · published research

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy

One randomized study found smaller postoperative day-three rises in ALT, AST, and ESR after red LED exposure to the gallbladder bed and porta hepatis. It did not establish a patient-centered recovery benefit.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One randomized study found smaller postoperative day-three rises in ALT, AST, and ESR after red LED exposure to the gallbladder bed and porta hepatis. It did not establish a patient-centered recovery benefit.

Summary of the Evidence

One open-label, single-centre randomized trial included 263 patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. It compared usual surgery with or without a single intraoperative red-LED exposure to the gallbladder bed and porta hepatis. No duplicate report, animal experiment, or in-vitro study was identified. The trial measured blood markers three days after surgery rather than establishing a broader set of clinical recovery outcomes.

Human and clinical evidence

Postoperative increases in alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were smaller in the LED group than in controls. These are objective short-term laboratory outcomes, and the randomized comparison supports a treatment-associated difference. The publication did not establish that patients had less pain, fewer complications, shorter hospitalization, or better longer-term recovery. The size of the biomarker changes and their relationship to outcomes important to patients therefore remain unclear (Redkin et al. 2017).

Animal evidence

No animal study directly testing PBM during laparoscopic cholecystectomy was identified in the relevant indication records.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell-culture or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used a 625-nm red visible LED with pulse-width modulation at 76 Hz and a 23% duty cycle. Reported irradiance was 15–30 mW/cm² and fluence was 0.9–1.8 J/cm². Light was delivered once, after gallbladder removal, to the exposed operative bed and porta hepatis. This intraoperative route cannot be assumed to have the same effects as external treatment over intact skin. The study did not compare alternative wavelengths or doses.

Interpretation

The randomized study found smaller short-term rises in three postoperative blood markers after red LED exposure. This is a favorable biomarker result, but it does not by itself show that recovery was easier or complications were prevented. A blinded replication with pain, complications, length of stay, and validated recovery scores would establish whether the laboratory difference translates into a patient benefit.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for smaller short-term postoperative rises in ALT, AST, and ESR Very low for improved symptoms or fewer surgical complications
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One open-label randomized study of 263 patients found smaller day-three increases in liver enzymes and ESR after intraoperative red LED exposure. Randomization and sample size support the biomarker comparison, but the study did not establish better pain, complication, length-of-stay, or longer-term recovery outcomes. A blinded trial with patient-centered measures would clarify clinical relevance.
